title: IRDAI's May 25 Circular on Executive Pay: Six Mandatory Parameters Carry 50% of Variable Pay, Including Claims, Grievances and Dark Patterns
summary: IRDAI's circular of May 25, 2026, amending the 2024 Master Circular on Corporate Governance for Insurers, makes six performance parameters, covering financial soundness, product performance, claims responsiveness, grievance redressal, Indian Accounting Standards and removal of dark patterns, account for 50% of key managerial personnel variable pay from FY 2026-27 and requires public disclosure of the underlying data.
description:
India's insurance regulator has told insurers that the way they pay their most senior people must reflect how well they treat policyholders. The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India issued a circular dated May 25, 2026 that amends its Master Circular on Corporate Governance for Insurers, 2024. Outlook Money reported it on May 27, saying the changes apply from the 2026-27 financial year, and Legitpro Law summarised it for Mondaq on June 3. The circular is therefore a late-May measure, ahead of the 2026-27 pay cycle it is meant to shape. The Mondaq article does not reproduce the circular or give a circular reference number, so the details here come from that and other published summaries.

The core of the change is a scorecard for key management personnel, the senior executives such as the chief executive and heads of key functions. According to Mondaq, six mandatory parameters together account for fifty percent of the total assessment used for variable pay and incentives. The six are overall financial soundness, product performance, claims responsiveness, grievance redressal, implementation of Indian Accounting Standards, and the removal of dark patterns in insurer and distributor interactions with customers. Outlook Money gives the weights of two of them, 10% each for implementing Indian Accounting Standards and for removing dark patterns, and says the remaining 50% of the variable pay weighting is set by insurers according to their business priorities and each executive's role. It names the factors for evaluating executives as speed of claim settlement, responsiveness to policyholders, grievance resolution efficiency and product performance. Neither summary gives the weights of the other parameters.

Dark patterns are website or app designs that can confuse customers or steer them into decisions they would not otherwise make. Including them in the executive scorecard puts the digital sales process, which has been a source of complaints, within the leadership's responsibility.

The circular also forces disclosure. Outlook Money reports that insurers must publish data on claims, such as the share of claims settled within 15, 30 and 60 days and beyond, and how many were fully paid, partially paid, rejected, repudiated or still pending. They must publish complaints resolved within set timelines and those still unresolved. Routine service requests and grievances should be kept separate, and a service request unresolved for more than seven days may need to be treated as a grievance. Claims, product performance and grievance data must be published monthly, and financial soundness data quarterly, on the insurer's website in a simple, accessible format, without requiring visitors to provide personal details. Mondaq adds that insurers must disclose the parameters behind executive remuneration, publicly report performance against them and make historical data available in an accessible format.

The metrics differ by type of insurer. For life insurers, Outlook Money lists renewal premium ratios, persistency levels, expense management and assets under management. For general and standalone health insurers, it lists incurred loss ratios, renewal business ratios and expense management indicators. Mondaq notes that sector-specific financial metrics now apply to life, general and health insurers, without giving figures. Persistency, a measure of how many customers keep their policies, appears in the earlier framework and not among the revised mandatory parameters in the Mondaq summary, though Outlook Money lists it for life insurers' disclosure.

Governance is part of the design. Boards and remuneration committees must show that executive incentives reflect policyholder interests, conduct risk and long-term governance objectives. Outlook Money adds that nomination and remuneration committees must coordinate with risk management committees when designing senior management pay. The summaries do not state a penalty for non-compliance, and they do not state deferral or clawback rules for variable pay, so those points should be checked in the circular itself.

The reaction in published coverage is limited. Outlook Money attributes a view to unnamed industry experts that the move could push insurers to improve customer servicing, since weak claim settlement or rising unresolved complaints may now affect executive incentives, and it quotes no named person or insurer. Law-firm commentary frames the circular as a form of indirect enforcement: instead of fining the company, the regulator changes what executives are rewarded for. Critics of such an approach could argue that pay set by regulator-defined measures reduces companies' commercial discretion, but the summaries reviewed do not record a named critic.

The design also reflects a view that conduct problems in insurance are partly incentive problems. When bonuses depend mainly on growth or profit, weaker claims handling or complaint resolution can look like a cost saving, and a scorecard that carries service measures changes that calculation for the people deciding how resources are allocated. Whether it works will depend on how rigorously boards score executives against the published data. For policyholders, the visible effect should be data. Once the monthly claims and grievance figures appear on insurers' websites, comparing insurers becomes easier. For insurers, the immediate work is building the scorecard, the reporting pipeline and the board oversight before the financial year's pay decisions. Readers who need the exact weights, definitions and transition rules should read the circular itself.
source_name: Mondaq (June 3, 2026), Outlook Money (May 27, 2026) and law-firm commentary on the IRDAI circular of May 25, 2026
image_alt: Insurance policy paperwork representing regulatory pay reforms (illustrative)
key_points: IRDAI issued the circular on May 25, 2026, amending its Master Circular on Corporate Governance for Insurers, 2024; Outlook Money reports the changes apply from FY 2026-27.

Six mandatory parameters together make up 50% of the assessment used for variable pay: overall financial soundness, product performance, claims responsiveness, grievance redressal, implementation of Indian Accounting Standards and removal of dark patterns; the other 50% is set by insurers.

Insurers must publish claims data, such as the share settled within 15, 30 and 60 days and beyond, and the number paid, partly paid, rejected, repudiated or pending, monthly, and financial soundness data quarterly, on their websites without asking users for personal details.

Boards and nomination and remuneration committees must show that executive incentives reflect policyholder interests, conduct risk and long-term governance and coordinate with risk management committees.

Sector metrics differ: life insurers report items such as renewal premium ratios, persistency and assets under management, while general and standalone health insurers report incurred loss ratios, renewal business ratios and expense indicators.
why_it_matters: Executives respond to how they are paid. By tying half of variable pay to measures that include claims responsiveness and complaint handling, the regulator is trying to make customer outcomes matter to the people who run insurers. The disclosure rules matter as much as the pay rules, because published monthly claims data lets policyholders, journalists and analysts compare insurers. Industry commentary notes the risk of more regulatory involvement in commercial decisions; the circular does not, as summarised, specify deferral or clawback, so how strongly it bites will depend on how boards apply it.

title: Health Insurance Is 61% of India's Insurance Ombudsman Complaints but 11% of Premiums, and IRDAI Still Cannot Say Why Claims Are Denied
summary: Health insurance rose from 38.64% of insurance complaints in FY20 to 61.49% in FY25 while representing 10.68% of premiums, Lok Sabha replies show health complaints of 47,658, 64,365 and 73,729 (to February) in FY24 to FY26, and a July 2026 reply confirmed IRDAI collects overall repudiation rates (8% of 3.26 crore claims) but not the reasons for denials.
description:
Health insurance is the part of India's insurance market that generates the most complaints relative to its size, and the regulator's data show that it has been getting worse. Business Standard, in a "Datanomics" analysis published on June 9, 2026 that attributes its data to the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, reports that insurance complaints nearly doubled over six years since FY20 and that the growth was driven largely by health insurance. Health's share of complaints rose from 38.64% in FY20 to 61.49% in FY25. Health insurance accounts for only 10.68% of total insurance premiums, so its complaint share is more than six times its premium share. Life insurance, by contrast, has close to three-quarters of total premiums but about 30% of complaints. The article says insurance ombudsmen resolved 41,055 grievances in FY26. It does not say whether that figure counts complaints filed or resolved beyond using the word resolved, and it does not name the IRDAI report from which the data come.

Parliament has been given consistent numbers. CafeMutual reported on April 1, 2026 that a written reply by the Minister of State for Finance, Pankaj Chaudhary, to a Lok Sabha question gave health insurance complaints of 47,658 in FY24, 64,365 in FY25 and 73,729 in FY26 up to February 2026. The FY26 figure covers roughly eleven months, so the full-year total will be higher. The Business Standard analysis ranks Star Health at the top of the complaints chart among general and health insurers, with a complaint share nearly three times its premium share, and National Insurance, a public sector insurer, second. Mumbai and Pune together account for nearly 20% of annual complaint filings.

The claims figures come from a later reply. Insurance Business Asia reported on July 27, 2026 on a Lok Sabha reply delivered on July 24, which cited IRDAI's annual report for 2024-25. Indian insurers processed 3.26 crore, or 32.6 million, health claims in the year ending March 2025. Of these, 87% were settled and 8% were repudiated, meaning roughly one claim in twelve was not paid, and about 5% were still pending at year end. The article states that IRDAI "holds no data on why those claims are denied": the regulator collects only overall repudiation rates, not the reasons for individual denials, and insurer-wise data on claims rejected on grounds such as "non-medical necessity" or "exclusion" over the past three years is not available. In an earlier reply, the minister said there is no specific category for hospitalisation claims rejected because the treatment was classed as out-patient care, so the system does not record them separately. The government also said it has no proposal to require insurers to give the treating doctor's opinion overriding precedence, because a doctor's opinion is one input among several that insurers weigh, with clinical records, medical standards, treatment protocols and policy conditions.

The grievance system has its own figures. Bima Bharosa, the regulator's complaint platform, recorded 257,790 complaints in FY2024-25, up about 20% from 215,569 the previous year, and claim-related issues made up about 69% of grievances for general and health insurers. The 17 insurance ombudsman offices received 53,184 complaints in FY2024-25, according to the Council for Insurance Ombudsmen annual report, and about 71% were resolved in the policyholder's favour. Health disputes were about 64% of ombudsman complaints, life about 24% and motor about 9%. Because these figures are measured on different bases, they should not be added to or compared directly with the Business Standard percentages, which describe the share of complaints in the regulator's data over time.

Reforms have targeted process rather than reasons. The article lists the Master Circular on Protection of Policyholders' Interests, 2024, mandatory customer information sheets, a 30-day free-look period, one-hour cashless pre-authorisation decisions and three-hour discharge authorisation timelines. None of these requires insurers to disclose, or IRDAI to collect, insurer-wise reasons for individual claim denials. In May 2025, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman directed public sector general insurers to adopt AI-driven claim settlement for motor own damage and health insurance. Insurance penetration fell to 3.7% of GDP in FY2024 from 4% in FY2022-23 and 4.2% during the pandemic years, and WTW projects Asia-Pacific medical cost increases of 14% in 2026, up from 13.2% in 2025.

A related development is IRDAI's May 25, 2026 circular linking executive pay to claims responsiveness and grievance redressal, which will require insurers to publish monthly claims and grievance data. That could address part of the information gap, although the sources reviewed do not say it will require reasons for rejection.

For policyholders, the practical advice that follows from the data is modest: keep treatment records and correspondence, read exclusions and waiting periods before buying, escalate unresolved complaints through the insurer's grievance process and, if necessary, the ombudsman. For regulators, the figures suggest that understanding why one claim in twelve is repudiated would be a useful next step.
source_name: Business Standard (June 9, 2026), CafeMutual (April 1, 2026) and Insurance Business Asia (July 27, 2026)
image_alt: Hospital paperwork and stethoscope representing health insurance claims (illustrative)
key_points: Business Standard reports health insurance's share of insurance complaints rose from 38.64% in FY20 to 61.49% in FY25, against 10.68% of total premiums; life insurance has close to three-quarters of premiums but about 30% of complaints, and insurance ombudsmen resolved 41,055 grievances in FY26.

Lok Sabha replies put health insurance complaints at 47,658 in FY24, 64,365 in FY25 and 73,729 in FY26 to February 2026; Star Health tops the complaints chart among general and health insurers, followed by National Insurance, and Mumbai and Pune account for nearly 20% of annual filings.
A July 24, 2026 reply cited IRDAI's 2024-25 annual report: 3.26 crore health claims were processed, 87% settled, 8% repudiated and about 5% pending at year end.

IRDAI collects only overall repudiation rates, not the reasons for individual denials; insurer-wise data on rejections for 'non-medical necessity' or exclusions is not available, and no category records hospitalisation claims rejected as out-patient care.

Bima Bharosa recorded 257,790 complaints in FY25, up about 20%, with claim issues about 69% of general and health grievances; the 17 ombudsman offices received 53,184 complaints, about 71% resolved in the policyholder's favour.
why_it_matters: Health insurance is the product where Indian customers most often feel let down, and the figures show the gap between its share of complaints and its share of premiums is wide. The regulator can see how many claims are rejected but not why, which limits how well it can tell whether denials are justified or a sign of mis-selling or poor processing. The reforms it has introduced, such as faster cashless approvals, address delays but not the reasons for denials. Policyholders should keep records of treatment and correspondence and know that the ombudsman route exists; the data suggest it frequently rules for the policyholder.

title: UK Motor Finance Redress Scheme: Upper Tribunal Hearing Set for February 16-26, 2027 as Lenders Need Not Calculate or Pay Compensation Until Four Legal Challenges Are Decided, With November 18 Notification Deadline Still Live
summary: The FCA's motor finance redress scheme, established on March 30, 2026, has been partially suspended while the Upper Tribunal hears four legal challenges from February 16 to 26, 2027, meaning lenders need not calculate or pay redress until the case ends, though they must still identify complaints and notify those not owed compensation, with the first deadline on November 18, 2026.
description:
The Financial Conduct Authority's motor finance redress scheme is moving through the legal system, not through payments. The FCA established the Motor Finance Commission Consumer Redress Scheme on March 30, 2026, using powers in sections 404 and 404A of the Financial Services and Markets Act. Four parties then challenged its lawfulness before the Upper Tribunal, and the Tribunal partly suspended the scheme. This article uses the FCA's legal challenge documents page as it stood on October 26, 2026, and reporting on the FCA's statement of October 13, 2026. The FCA page does not say which provisions are suspended, and this article does not claim to list them.

The challengers

The FCA's page names four applicants challenging the scheme under section 404D(1) of FSMA: CA Auto Finance UK Limited, Consumer Voice Limited, Mercedes-Benz Financial Services UK Limited, and Volkswagen Financial Services (UK) Limited. The Upper Tribunal, Tax and Chancery Chamber, has jurisdiction. Each applicant has published an application and a statement of grounds, and the FCA has published its grounds of response. Replies from the four applicants were added on September 1, 2026. According to the reporting reviewed, the FCA announced on May 1, 2026 that it had received the four challenges and that none was expressly brought in the name of individual consumers.

The suspension

The Tribunal suspended parts of the scheme on terms agreed between the FCA and the four challengers. The FCA's page dates the suspension order July 1, 2026, and lists a separate directions order of the same date. Other reporting gives July 2. The sources do not explain the discrepancy, and the FCA page, as the regulator's own record, is followed here for the order date. Which date is right does not change the effect described below.

The hearing

Directions issued after applications were heard on October 5 and 6, 2026. The FCA confirmed on October 13 that the Upper Tribunal will hear the four challenges from February 16 to 26, 2027. The final hearing is listed for nine days from February 16, with four additional days of judicial pre-reading. Further directions on expert evidence and disclosure were issued on October 12 and October 26. A judgment is expected in the months after the hearing.

What firms must and need not do

Under the partial suspension, lenders do not have to calculate or pay redress, or send compensation communications, until the Tribunal process concludes. They must still identify relevant complaints and agreements, gather data and tell complainants who are not owed compensation, subject to limited exceptions.

Two notification deadlines apply. The first is November 18, 2026, covering agreements from April 1, 2014 and complaints made by June 30, 2026. The second is January 18, 2027, covering earlier agreements and complaints made by August 31, 2026. Complaints made after those dates must be answered within five months. The FCA told firms to keep preparing and to progress complaints as far as possible.

If the scheme is quashed

The FCA has told lenders to plan for the possibility that the scheme is quashed in whole or in part. In that case, according to the reporting, there could be no motor finance compensation scheme and no pause on complaint handling. The FCA said lenders should hold appropriate capital and liquidity and warned that it could impose business restrictions otherwise. This is the regulator's guidance to firms, and the outcome of the hearing has not been decided.

Scale and timing

Reporting on the FCA's statements says the scheme is expected to return about £7.5 billion to consumers and that the vast majority of claims should be settled by the end of 2027. The same reporting says motor finance borrowing was £39 billion in 2024. These are the FCA's estimates and context figures, not outcomes. The reporting describes the period covered as running from 2007 to 2024, while the notification deadlines above refer to agreements from April 1, 2014 and earlier agreements, so the exact eligibility rules should be checked in the scheme rules and the FCA's policy statement, PS26/3.

The FCA described the scheme in March as "the quickest, fairest and most efficient way to compensate consumers" and said it will defend it robustly.

Advice for consumers

The reporting says that complaining to a lender is free, and that claims management firms may charge up to 36% of compensation. Customers who made a complaint should watch for a letter from their lender, particularly around the notification deadlines. A letter saying no compensation is owed is not necessarily the end of the matter, and the FCA's materials explain how complainants can respond, which this article has not reviewed in detail.

What is not known

The sources do not say which scheme provisions are suspended in detail, do not give the reasons for each challenger's case beyond the pleadings' existence, and do not say what the Tribunal will decide. Anyone relying on this timeline should check the FCA page for updates, because directions are issued regularly.
source_name: Financial Conduct Authority (legal challenge documents page, as of October 26, 2026), with reporting on the FCA's October 13, 2026 statement
image_alt: Legal documents representing a financial redress scheme (illustrative)
key_points: The FCA established the Motor Finance Commission Consumer Redress Scheme on March 30, 2026 under sections 404 and 404A of FSMA, and four parties are challenging its lawfulness before the Upper Tribunal: CA Auto Finance UK, Consumer Voice, Mercedes-Benz Financial Services UK and Volkswagen Financial Services (UK).
The Tribunal partly suspended the scheme on terms agreed with the challengers; the FCA's page dates the suspension order July 1, 2026, while other reporting dates it July 2.
The final hearing is listed for nine days from February 16, 2027, with a window of February 16 to 26, and a judgment is expected in the months after.

Until the process concludes, firms need not calculate or pay redress or send compensation communications, but must still identify relevant complaints and agreements, gather data and tell complainants who are not owed compensation, with notification deadlines of November 18, 2026 and January 18, 2027.

The FCA told lenders to plan for the scheme being quashed in whole or part, in which case there could be no scheme and no pause on complaint handling, and said the vast majority of claims should still be settled by the end of 2027.
why_it_matters: Millions of people with car finance agreements may be owed compensation, and lenders have set aside large sums, so the timing of the legal process decides when money could reach consumers and whether the scheme survives in its current form. The notification deadlines also matter to customers who have complained and been told they are not owed anything.

title: MAS Publishes 'SAFR' White Paper With Industry on Runtime Safeguards for AI Agents in Finance: Identity, Controls, a Disposition Engine and Tamper-Evident Audit Logs
summary: On July 3, 2026 the Monetary Authority of Singapore published an industry white paper, 'Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime' (SAFR), developed with financial institutions and fintechs, describing four runtime components that keep AI agents within the mandates and risk limits set by their firms.
description:
Artificial intelligence systems that can carry out tasks on their own, often called AI agents, are starting to appear in finance. They might initiate a payment, rebalance a portfolio or answer a client and take an action on the client's behalf. Singapore's financial regulator has now published a technical blueprint for keeping them under control. According to an analysis by the law firm Rajah & Tann Asia dated July 6, 2026, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) published an industry white paper on July 3, 2026, titled "Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime", abbreviated to SAFR.

It is worth being clear about what SAFR is. The Rajah & Tann article describes it as an industry white paper, developed by MAS together with leading financial institutions and financial technology companies. The sources reviewed do not say whether it is open for formal consultation or whether it sets binding requirements, so it should be read as guidance and a reference design, not as a rule.

The paper's purpose is to give financial institutions real-time safeguards, so that AI agents stay within the mandates, policies and risk boundaries the institutions set. The central idea is that checks should operate at runtime, at the moment an agent proposes an action, rather than relying only on testing before deployment. The paper's own formulation, quoted by Rajah & Tann, is that "no agentic action reaches execution without having been declared, authorised and assessed."

SAFR describes four runtime components that work through what it calls a governance envelope. The first is agent identity. Each proposed action is checked against a registered agent, so that the institution knows which agent is acting and whether it is permitted to act. The second is a controls repository, which is the institution's configurable rulebook: the limits, policies and conditions that apply to agents. The third is a disposition engine, which resolves each action into one of four outcomes: deny, escalate, auto-execute or observe. Escalation is where a human gets involved, so the engine decides which actions can run automatically, which need a person's decision and which must be blocked. The fourth is an audit log, described as a tamper-evident, append-only record of governance decisions. Because entries can only be added and any alteration is detectable, the log allows later review of what an agent did and why it was allowed.

The framework builds on MAS's Project MindForge AI Risk Management toolkit, which connects it to the regulator's wider work on AI. That includes the guidelines on AI risk management that MAS proposed in November 2025, covering governance, an inventory of AI uses, risk materiality assessment and lifecycle controls for generative AI and AI agents, with a proposed 12-month transition period after issue. SAFR can be read as a technical complement to those principles: the guidelines say what a firm should have in place, and the white paper shows one way to build it for agents that act.

The paper identifies use cases: agent-assisted payments and treasury operations, wealth management and advisory workflows, and client engagement. These are areas where an agent's mistake can have direct financial consequences or affect customers, which is why the authorisation and escalation steps matter. The sources do not mention insurance claims or underwriting specifically, though the same design could apply to any regulated firm that deploys agents.

A few things the sources do not report. The article does not describe a regulatory sandbox, specific technical standards, deadlines for firms or enforcement. It does not give details of which institutions took part. Readers should therefore avoid assuming that adopting SAFR is mandatory or that following it would satisfy any regulatory requirement; that is a question for MAS and the firms' own supervisors.

Why does the approach matter? Traditional AI models produce predictions or recommendations that a person then acts upon. Agentic systems can carry out the next step, which raises questions of accountability, control and auditability. If an agent makes a payment error, a firm needs to know which agent acted, under whose authority and according to which rule. The design separates the agent from the rulebook that governs it, so that limits can be changed centrally and applied consistently, and it records decisions in a way that is hard to alter. A tamper-evident log is especially useful for regulators and auditors, who must reconstruct events after an incident.

Singapore's approach is consistent with its stated preference for principles-based supervision combined with practical industry collaboration. By publishing a reference design with industry participants, MAS offers a common vocabulary that firms can adopt or adapt, and signals the kind of controls it expects to see as agents spread. For firms elsewhere, including insurers and banks in jurisdictions that have not yet issued specific guidance, SAFR provides a concrete example of what runtime governance can look like.

The practical next steps for firms considering agents are to inventory where agents are used or planned, decide which actions an agent may take on its own, define the escalation triggers, and make sure logs are kept in a form that supports audit. Whether MAS follows the white paper with formal guidance or supervisory expectations is something to watch.
source_name: Rajah & Tann Asia (analysis of the MAS white paper, July 6, 2026) and Monetary Authority of Singapore
image_alt: Digital network graphic representing AI agents in finance (illustrative)
key_points: MAS published the white paper 'Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime' (SAFR) on July 3, 2026, developed with leading financial institutions and fintech companies; it is a white paper, not a rulebook.
SAFR describes four runtime components working through a 'governance envelope': agent identity, a controls repository, a disposition engine and an audit log.
The disposition engine resolves each proposed action to deny, escalate, auto-execute or observe, and the audit log is a tamper-evident, append-only record of governance decisions.
The paper states that no agentic action reaches execution without having been declared, authorised and assessed, and it builds on MAS's Project MindForge AI Risk Management toolkit.
Use cases include agent-assisted payments and treasury operations, wealth management and advisory workflows, and client engagement.
why_it_matters: AI agents that can take actions, not just give advice, raise new questions about who is accountable if something goes wrong. SAFR gives banks, insurers and fintechs a concrete design for keeping agents inside approved limits with records that can be audited.

title: OSFI's 2026-27 Annual Risk Outlook Ranks Mortgage Risk First, Warns 1.3 Million Mortgages Face Renewal Payment Shock, and Keeps Its 4.5x Loan-to-Income Limit Framework
summary: Canada's banking and insurance supervisor ranks residential mortgage risk first in its Annual Risk Outlook for April 2026 to April 2027, followed by non-bank financial institutions and funding and liquidity, notes that 1.3 million mortgages face first-time renewal at higher payments, and says its loan-to-income limit framework has met its prudential objectives.
description:
Canada's Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) has published its Annual Risk Outlook for fiscal year 2026-2027, which covers April 1, 2026 to April 1, 2027. The page's metadata lists an issue date of April 10, 2026 and the text gives April 14, 2026, so this article describes it as published in April 2026. OSFI regulates federally regulated banks, insurers and pension plans. The outlook sets out the risks it expects to focus on and what it plans to do about them. It does not give numeric ratings; the ranking of risks is the only ordering it provides.

The ranking

OSFI lists four groups of risks in order of importance. First is real estate secured lending, which covers mortgages and other loans backed by property. Second is risk from non-bank financial institutions. Third is funding and liquidity. Fourth is a group of other risks that includes wholesale credit, commercial real estate, artificial intelligence, cyber, third-party and integrity and security risks. The introduction refers to three key risks while the top-risks section lists four, with other risks as the fourth, so readers should not be surprised by the difference.

Mortgages and the renewal wave

The outlook puts a number on the pressure facing households. About 3.1 million mortgages, 52% of the total, will renew by the end of 2027. Of these, 1.3 million mortgages, 22% of the total, are fixed-rate loans or variable-rate loans with fixed payments that are renewing for the first time since they were taken out in 2021 and 2022. OSFI says these borrowers will face material payment increases. Variable-rate loans with fixed payments made up 36% of mortgage flows as of December 2025, close to the 41% high in March 2022.

OSFI also notes that condominium markets in Toronto and Vancouver are strained, with sales at levels not seen since the 1990s. It expects more residential mortgage arrears or defaults over the next two years, but does not expect losses on real estate secured lending to materially affect capital at most lenders. In other words, it expects more borrower stress, not a threat to the stability of most banks.

The loan-to-income limits

In 2025 OSFI introduced institution-specific portfolio limits on uninsured mortgage originations with a loan-to-income ratio above 4.5 times. In January 2026 it announced that the framework would continue. The outlook states that the loan-to-income limit framework has met its prudential objectives.

Non-bank lenders and trade-related credit risk

The second-ranked risk concerns non-bank financial institutions, which include hedge funds and private capital firms. OSFI says they can transmit stress through leverage, margin calls and interconnected exposures. Canadian institutions lend to these firms and the exposures have grown considerably. Banks also use them for credit protection through synthetic risk transfers, which may weaken in stress.

On trade, the page notes weak business sentiment and unsettled Canada-U.S. tariff negotiations, and says commercial real estate remains vulnerable, particularly high-rise condominium construction and development. It does not give specific loss estimates.

Funding, liquidity, cyber and AI

OSFI says institutions have enjoyed a stable funding environment over the past year, but geopolitical shocks, dependence on foreign-currency funding and a loss of confidence could tighten liquidity quickly. Revised liquidity adequacy requirements for certain retail deposit categories were due to take effect on May 1, 2026. On technology, malicious cyber activity is a significant threat and AI-enabled tools increase its speed and scale; software vulnerabilities are expected to remain the most persistent, high-impact technology risk, and AI adoption creates more vulnerability points. Operational resilience expectations take effect on September 1, 2026.

What it says about insurers

For insurers, the outlook lists several concerns. OSFI will monitor resilience to catastrophe risk for all insurers. Market volatility and growth in private-market assets raise concerns because those assets can be more opaque and potentially illiquid. Lapses and surrenders at life insurers have become more volatile, although losses remain modest relative to capital. Property and casualty insurers face claims inflation, notably in auto, and a softening commercial lines market that pressures underwriting. OSFI also points to cyber insurance underwriting, the use of AI in underwriting and mortgage insurers' exposure to the housing market. The climate-related work described in the outlook, including the 2026 Climate Risk Return and a catastrophic physical risk review, applies to banks, so it should not be read as a new insurer climate review.

What OSFI plans to do

Planned actions include supervisory reviews of lenders with significant real estate secured lending exposures and a new Credit Risk Management Guideline; reviews of non-bank exposures, synthetic risk transfers and hedge fund leverage, plus a loan-level wholesale data call; reviews of contingency funding and recovery plans and a draft internal liquidity adequacy assessment guideline; intelligence-led cyber resilience testing and a fourth third-party data call; continued monitoring of AI; and quarterly monitoring of wholesale credit risk.

What it means

For borrowers facing a renewal, the practical point is that payments may rise and it is worth talking to the lender early. For lenders and insurers, the outlook is a guide to supervisory attention. It is a forward-looking assessment, not a forecast of losses, and it can change. Readers who need the exact wording should consult OSFI's page. This article is general information and not financial advice.
source_name: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (Annual Risk Outlook, fiscal year 2026-2027)
image_alt: House and financial documents representing mortgage lending oversight (illustrative)
key_points: OSFI ranks its top risks as real estate secured lending and mortgage risk, non-bank financial institution risk, and funding and liquidity risk, with wholesale credit, commercial real estate, AI, cyber, third-party and integrity risks grouped as other risks.

About 3.1 million mortgages, or 52% of the total, renew by the end of 2027, and 1.3 million of them (22%) are fixed-rate or variable-rate-with-fixed-payment loans renewing for the first time since 2021-2022 and facing material payment increases.

OSFI introduced institution-specific limits on uninsured mortgage originations above a 4.5x loan-to-income ratio in 2025, announced in January 2026 that the framework will continue, and said it 'has met our prudential objectives'.

For insurers, OSFI cites catastrophe losses, volatile life insurance lapses and surrenders, claims inflation (notably auto), a softening commercial market, private-market asset opacity, and cyber and AI underwriting.
The outlook was published in April 2026 (page metadata lists April 10, the text April 14) and covers April 1, 2026 to April 1, 2027.
why_it_matters: OSFI supervises Canada's federally regulated banks, insurers and pension plans, so its ranking of risks shows where examiners will look. For homeowners the main point is the large wave of mortgage renewals at higher payments; for insurers it signals continued attention to catastrophe, claims inflation and private-market investments.
